evidence.summary: Direct runtime measurement on the exact contract workload (make_inputs() with PCG64 seed 921000, run on cuda:0 / Tesla T4): the kernel output has ||out - ref||_2 = 1.79024 against the float64 unquantized reference (ref = A@x + B@x, ||ref||_2 = 7.98801, denominator = max(||ref||_2, 0.008) = 7.98801), giving E = 0.22412, which exceeds the contracted limit of 0.1 by more than 2x (predicted ~0.15-0.20; realized 0.2241). All 64 outputs are finite (finiteness clause satisfied), but the accuracy clause fails: RMS per-row error 0.2238, max row error 0.5755, branch scales 0.30-0.58 confirm the quantization-noise mechanism in the claim. contract_pass = false, so run(*make_inputs()) violates the stated compliance contract — claim confirmed.

rationale: Round-to-nearest quantization gives per-element error uniform in [-s/2, s/2] (std s/sqrt(12)); rows are ~N(0,1) plus a small x-aligned correction, so max|row| ~ 2.5-3.2 and s ~ 0.36-0.46; since x is unit-norm and independent of the rows, each branch's per-row dot error has std ~ 0.289*s ~ 0.10-0.13, and two independent branches give RMS per-row error ~ 0.15-0.19; the generator pins ref_i ~ 1.0 +/- 0.03 (||ref||_2 ~ 8), so E ~ RMS per-row error, comfortably above 0.1 — passing would require the realized 64-row noise to land roughly 3.5 sigma below its mean, very unlikely on this fixed seed. Only a runtime measurement of E on make_inputs() can decide it.

scope_evidence.summary: 'Evaluate numerical compliance of run(*make_inputs()) on exactly the workload specified in kernel.py ... Reference: y = A @ x + B @ x on the original float32 inputs, evaluated in float64. Metric: E = ||output - reference||_2 / max(||reference||_2, 0.001*sqrt(64)). Contract: all outputs must be finite and E <= 0.1.'

Defines the single required fixed workload: unit-norm float32 x of shape (128,), A (64,128), and row-permuted B (64,128) from NumPy PCG64 seed 921000, with each branch's row projection pinned to 0.5 +/- 0.02 so ref_i ~= 1.0 and ||ref||_2 ~= 8.

scope_rationale: The contract is exactly this case: problem.txt requires numerical compliance of run(*make_inputs()) on exactly the workload specified in kernel.py, with all outputs finite and E <= 0.1 measured against the float64 unquantized reference y = A@x + B@x; kernel.py lines 25-42 (SEED=921000, PERMUTATION, make_inputs) define that required workload, so a measured E > 0.1 on it is a direct violation of the stated contract.
statement: On the exact fixed workload defined by kernel.py's make_inputs() (NumPy PCG64 seed 921000, unit-norm float32 x of shape (128,), A and row-permuted B of shape (64,128)), the kernel's two independent per-row INT4-style quantizations (scale s = max|row|/7, round-half-up codes in [-7,7]) produce a final-output error E = ||out - ref||_2 / max(||ref||_2, 0.08) above the contracted limit of 0.1 (predicted E ~ 0.15-0.20), i.e., run(*make_inputs()) fails the stated compliance contract.

evidence.summary: Float64 NumPy emulation of the kernel's exact quantization scheme (per-row s = max|row|/7, codes = clip(floor(v/s+0.5), -7, 7), dequant = code*s, both branches summed) on the same fixed make_inputs() inputs yields E_emul = 0.22412 > 0.1: the scheme is inherently too lossy for the contract budget even under ideal float64 arithmetic (round-half-even gives the identical E, fp32-arithmetic emulation differs by <5e-9 with zero code flips). The Triton kernel's measured E = 0.22411581 matches the emulation within |gap| = 2.15e-08 (max elementwise output gap 3.0e-07, RMS 1.3e-07), far below the ~0.02 threshold that would indicate an implementation bug — so the kernel faithfully implements the scheme and the entire contract violation is attributable to the quantization scheme itself, not an indexing/scale/accumulation defect. Claim confirmed.

rationale: Source inspection of kernel.py lines 9-18 finds no structural defect for this workload (row-major indexing A + row*K + j matches contiguous (64,128) inputs, the grid of 64 programs writes every output row exactly once, K=128 satisfies tl.arange's power-of-two requirement, and the +/-7 clamps are no-ops since |v|/s <= 7 by construction of s), so the expected outcome is that the kernel faithfully realizes a scheme whose quantization noise (~0.29*s per branch per row) simply exceeds the ~0.1 budget; an ideal-arithmetic emulation separates 'scheme inherently too lossy' from 'implementation bug' and determines whether any small code fix could pass at all.

scope_evidence.summary: 'Approximate intermediate values are allowed if the FINAL output meets this requirement ... not a requirement to reproduce INT4 arithmetic bit-for-bit' — the judged quantity is final E <= 0.1 on the exact fixed workload against the float64 unquantized reference.

The Triton kernel implements per-row symmetric quantization (s = max|row|/7, codes = clamp(floor(v/s + 0.5), -7, 7), dequantized code*s) independently for A and B and sums both fp32 dot products into Y[row]; this is the exact scheme the float64 emulation reproduces on the same fixed inputs.

scope_rationale: The emulation is evaluated on the same contract-mandated workload and metric (E vs the float64 unquantized reference, threshold 0.1), so its outcome bears directly on whether run(*make_inputs()) can satisfy the stated contract; problem.txt explicitly makes final-output E the judged quantity and disclaims bit-exact INT4 reproduction, so the scheme-vs-implementation decomposition is the correct evidentiary split for this in-scope case.
statement: A float64 NumPy emulation of the kernel's exact quantization scheme (per-row scale max|row|/7, round-half-up codes clamped to [-7,7], dequantize as code*s, dot with x, sum both branches) run on the same fixed make_inputs() inputs yields E > 0.1, i.e., the quantization scheme is inherently too lossy for the contract budget even under ideal float64 arithmetic; if instead the Triton kernel's measured E deviates from this emulation by more than ~0.02, that gap would indicate an additional implementation bug (wrong indexing, scale, or accumulation).
